title: Star Expansions and the Erdős–Hajnal Property

items.title: The star-expansion of a graph
A wide coherent blockade contains a blockade-rainbow copy of a forest
items.strategy: Pass from the forest to a tree containing it and apply the pure-pairs rainbow-tree theorem to the blockade, rewriting the coherence hypothesis in the width-normalized form used there. The resulting rainbow tree contains the required rainbow forest as an induced subgraph.

items.title: Few induced copies force a linearly large induced subgraph with bounded maximum degree
items.strategy: Apply the published Nikiforov theorem to get a linearly large restricted induced subgraph. If the sparse side occurs, trim to the prescribed size with the sparse-subgraph lemma; if the dense side occurs, apply the same argument in the complement.

items.title: A long blockade without a large pure pair contains a rainbow forest or its complement
items.strategy: Count tuples using distinct blocks to show that the absence of a rainbow forest forces few induced copies on the blockade support. The bounded-degree corollary then yields a large low-degree induced subgraph of the support or of its complement; repack that set into fewer wider blocks and apply the rainbow-forest theorem unless a forbidden large pure pair already exists.

items.title: A long blockade yields a wide cograph-pattern subblockade or a rainbow forest
items.strategy: Induct on the target cograph depth. Apply the previous theorem to the current blockade; if it yields the rainbow outcome we are done, and otherwise a large pure pair splits the blockade into two long sides to which the induction hypothesis applies. Combining the two cograph-pattern outcomes across that pure split produces the required larger cograph-pattern blockade.

items.title: The star-expansion four-family of a forest has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Argue by a minimal counterexample in the kappa formulation. The published low-degree extraction theorem and the rooted stable-tooth comb theorem produce a large comb in a sparse induced subgraph; if that comb yields no rainbow copy of the forest or its complement, the long-blockade theorem gives a wide cograph-pattern subblockade, contradicting the published tau-critical obstruction. Therefore one rainbow copy occurs and lifts to one of the four star-expansion forbidden graphs.

items.title: The star-expansion of the four-vertex path and its complement have the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Apply the previous theorem with the forest $P_4$, using the published fact that $P_4$ is self-complementary so the four forbidden graphs collapse to the star-expansion and its complement.

items.title: The star-expansion of the four-vertex path contains induced six- and seven-cycles
items.strategy: Label the path vertices in order and inspect the star-expansion directly. One cycle uses the root, the two end teeth, and the four path vertices, while the other inserts both central teeth as well; the star-expansion definition excludes all potential chords.

items.title: The six-cycle and its complement have the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: The previous lemma shows that both $C_6$ and its complement occur inside the star-expansion of $P_4$ and its complement. Therefore the class forbidding $C_6$ and its complement is a hereditary subclass of the class forbidding that larger pair, so the Erdős–Hajnal property passes down.

items.title: The seven-cycle and its complement have the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Use the same subclass argument as for the six-cycle, now with the seven-cycle witness from the previous lemma. Since the star-expansion pair already has the Erdős–Hajnal property, the smaller forbidden pair inherits it.

items.title: A forest complement and its star-expansion have the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Repeat the tau-critical setup from the star-expansion four-family theorem, but keep track of the possibility that the low-degree subgraph lives in the complement. The published sparse-forest theorem rules out that complement-side case by forcing a large complete pair, and in the remaining case the same rooted-comb and rainbow-forest argument yields the star-expansion of the forest.

items.title: A star-expansion of a forest containing a long path contains the corresponding cycle
items.strategy: Take a path $b_1-\cdots-b_{r+1}$ inside the forest and use the vertices $v,a_1,b_1,\ldots,b_{r+1},a_{r+1}$ in the star-expansion. They form an induced cycle of length $r+4$ because only the two end teeth meet the root and each tooth only meets its matched path vertex.

items.title: A cycle and a forest complement have the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Choose a forest containing both the given forest and a path long enough that its star-expansion contains the desired cycle. The previous theorem gives the Erdős–Hajnal property for forbidding that forest complement together with the larger star-expansion, and the hereditary-subclass argument then passes the property to the smaller cycle-plus-forest-complement pair.

items.title: A hatted-five-cycle-free rooted stable-tooth comb yields a large pure blockade of components
items.strategy: Inside each comb block choose a large connected component by the same maximal-packing argument as in the source proof. If one chosen component were mixed on another, the root together with the two corresponding teeth and a short internal edge would realize the hatted five-cycle, so the chosen components form a pure blockade.

items.title: The star-expansion of $K_3$ contains the hatted five-cycle
items.strategy: Write the star-expansion of the triangle explicitly and pick the root, two teeth, two matched triangle vertices, and one extra triangle vertex. Their adjacencies are exactly those of a five-cycle with one extra vertex attached to two adjacent cycle vertices.

items.title: The hatted five-cycle and its complement have the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Again use a minimal kappa-counterexample and the rooted stable-tooth comb extracted from a sparse induced subgraph. The previous lemma turns the comb blocks into a large pure blockade of connected components, and the second finite witness lemma shows that a rainbow triangle in its pattern would already realize the hatted five-cycle. A classical triangle-free Ramsey bound therefore gives a large anticomplete subblockade, contradicting the tau-critical obstruction.

title: Star Expansions and the Erdős–Hajnal Property — Examples

items.title: The star-expansion of the four-vertex path
items.strategy: Write the path vertices as $b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4$, add the teeth $a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4$ and the root $v$, and list the edges prescribed by the definition. This is the figure used for the cycle consequences on the A page.

items.title: The star-expansion of the four-vertex path contains an induced five-cycle
items.strategy: In the previous graph, the vertices $v,a_1,b_1,b_2,b_3$ form a five-cycle. Checking the star-expansion adjacency list shows that no extra edge among those five vertices is present.

items.title: The star-expansion of the four-vertex path contains an induced six-cycle
items.strategy: Use the cycle $v-a_1-b_1-b_2-b_3-b_4-a_4-v$ with the central teeth omitted. The definition leaves exactly the displayed six edges among those vertices.

items.title: The star-expansion of the four-vertex path contains an induced seven-cycle
items.strategy: Use the cycle $v-a_1-b_1-b_2-b_3-b_4-a_4-v$ together with one central tooth to realize the seven-cycle check in the source figure. A direct adjacency audit shows the chosen seven vertices induce exactly that cycle.

items.title: The star-expansion of $K_3$ contains the hatted five-cycle
items.strategy: Take the explicit star-expansion of the triangle and mark the six-vertex induced subgraph used on the A page. Listing the adjacencies shows a five-cycle together with one extra vertex adjacent to two adjacent cycle vertices.

title: Iterative Sparsification and the Five-Vertex Path

items.title: A nice graph
Small anticonnected components yield a complete blockade
items.strategy: Take a minimal partition of the graph into unions of anticonnected components whose parts all have size below $|G|/k$. Minimality forces every noninitial part to have size at least $|G|/(2k)$, and distinct anticomponents are complete to one another, so the noninitial parts form the required blockade.

items.title: A dense bipartite side has a small hitting set
items.strategy: Choose about $1/x$ vertices from the dense side uniformly at random. The expected number of vertices on the other side missed by that sample is at most half of the side, so some sample hits at least half of it.

items.title: A sparse $P_5$-free graph has an anticomplete two-blockade
items.strategy: Take a large connected component and then a large connected component inside the set outside one chosen neighbourhood. Any remaining edge between the two large pieces would extend to an induced five-vertex path, so the two pieces are anticomplete.

items.title: A sparse $\overline{P_5}$-free graph has a large nearly covered sparse pair
items.strategy: Start from a high-degree vertex in the sparse graph and separate the neighbours from the far side. Deleting the exceptional vertices that see too much of the neighbourhood leaves a large set sparse to that neighbourhood, and deleting the neighbourhood vertices with too few reverse neighbours leaves a large subpair to which a small hitting set can be applied.

items.title: Anticonnected block contraction turns an upside-down comb into a pure blockade
items.strategy: Apply the published comb theorem on the small hitting set to obtain the upside-down comb. Then either one block already has a complete subblockade through the anticonnected-component lemma, or each block has a large anticonnected component; any mixed relation between two chosen components creates an induced $\overline{P_5}$ together with the root and one tooth.

items.title: A sparse $\overline{P_5}$-free graph either sparsifies further or yields a pure blockade or a large sparse pair
items.strategy: If the graph is already sparser there is nothing to do. Otherwise take a high-degree vertex, build the nearly covered sparse pair, hit many reverse neighbours by a small set, use the published comb theorem to extract the upside-down comb, and contract its blocks to the pure blockade provided by the previous lemma unless the large sparse-pair outcome has already appeared.

items.title: An $x$-sparse blockade iteration yields further sparsification or a pure blockade
items.strategy: Take a maximal $x$-sparse blockade whose last block remains large. Apply the previous lemma inside the last block. If the pure-blockade outcome occurs we are done, and if the sparse-pair outcome occurs it extends the maximal blockade, so only the further-sparsification outcome can survive.

items.title: An iterative sparsification step for sparse $\overline{P_5}$-free graphs
items.strategy: Choose the smallest density threshold $y$ for which the graph has a large $cy^3$-sparse induced subgraph. The previous blockade-iteration lemma applied there produces either a pure blockade of the right polynomial size or an $x$-sparse blockade at the next density scale, and the alternative deeper-sparsification outcome contradicts the minimal choice of $y$.

items.title: $\overline{P_5}$-free graphs admit a pure or $x$-sparse polynomial blockade
items.strategy: Use Rödl to pass to a large restricted induced subgraph of constant sparsity. If the sparse side lives in the complement, use the sparse $P_5$ lemma there to get an anticomplete two-blockade immediately; otherwise apply the iterative sparsification step inside a sparse side and translate the resulting blockade back to the original graph with the polynomial width bound.

items.title: A maximal layout has at most $\epsilon^{-1}$ blocks
items.strategy: If a layout already has at least $\epsilon^{-1}$ blocks, then the wrong-pair budget forces every nonedge of the pattern graph to correspond to a weakly sparse pair. The layout blocks themselves therefore form the required nice blockade.

items.title: Refining the largest layout block forces local blockade length at least $\epsilon^{-1}$
items.strategy: Refine the largest layout block by the pure or $x$-sparse blockade provided by the previous theorem. If the local blockade were too short, substituting its pattern into the layout would preserve every size and wrong-pair constraint while increasing the number of layout blocks, contradicting maximality.

items.title: Local pure or $x$-sparse blockades yield a nice blockade
items.strategy: Choose a maximal layout minimizing wrong pairs. The previous two lemmas force a large local blockade inside the largest block whose pattern can be substituted back into the layout without violating the wrong-pair budget. That substitution gives enough blocks that either the layout itself or the refined local blockade already has the length and weak-sparsity demanded by niceness.

items.title: The five-vertex path is nice
items.strategy: Apply the local blockade theorem to every $\overline{P_5}$-free graph with $x$ chosen as a fixed power of $\epsilon$. The pure or sparse blockade produced on every sufficiently large induced subgraph satisfies exactly the hypotheses of the local theorem, and the resulting blockade has the polynomial width and weak-sparsity exponents required in the definition of niceness.

items.title: A semisparse blockade can be sampled to anticonnected blocks with nearly pure relations
items.strategy: Start from the nice blockade for $P_5$ with a very small sparsity parameter and sample equal-size subsets from each block. Weak sparsity persists under sampling, and inside each sampled block either a large complete subblockade appears through the anticonnected-component lemma or a large anticonnected component survives; these choices give a new blockade whose cross-relations are complete or directionally sparse.

items.title: No vertex is mixed on many blocks of a semisparse blockade
items.strategy: If one outside vertex were mixed on too many sampled blocks, then those blocks could not contain a complete pair, because such a pair together with two appropriately chosen witnesses inside the mixed blocks would realize $\overline{P_5}$. Their union would therefore be sparse enough to trigger the deeper-sparsification outcome, contradicting the standing assumption of the enclosing lemma.

items.title: A sparse $\overline{P_5}$-free graph yields deeper sparsification or a complete blockade or a large anticomplete set
items.strategy: Use the sampled semisparse blockade from the previous lemma. If some outside vertex is mixed on many blocks, the union of those blocks is already sparser; otherwise one block has few mixed neighbours outside, and almost all outside vertices are anticomplete to it, giving the large anticomplete set unless the complete-blockade outcome already appears inside the block sequence.

items.title: A sparse $\overline{P_5}$-free graph yields a complete or anticomplete blockade or a sparser subgraph
items.strategy: Iterate the previous lemma along a maximal anticomplete blockade. If the complete or anticomplete blockade appears we are done; if only the large anticomplete-set outcome appears, append that set as a new block and contradict maximality. Hence the only surviving alternative is a deeper sparse induced subgraph.

items.title: The minimal sparsity parameter drops below the target
items.strategy: Choose a minimal sparsity threshold $y$ at which a large sparse induced subgraph exists but the desired complete or anticomplete blockade does not. Applying the previous lemma inside that subgraph rules out the blockade outcome, so the only remaining outcome is a sparser induced subgraph, contradicting minimality unless $y<x$.

items.title: $\overline{P_5}$-free graphs yield a polynomial restricted set or a complete or anticomplete blockade
items.strategy: Choose a minimal sparse induced subgraph at the density scale between $x$ and a fixed constant. The previous lemma forces that threshold below $x$, so the chosen induced subgraph is already $x$-sparse and polynomially large; otherwise the complete or anticomplete blockade outcome has appeared earlier. This yields exactly the two outcomes needed for the published blockade-to-restricted-subgraph theorem.

items.title: The five-vertex path has the polynomial Rödl property
items.strategy: Apply the previous theorem to every large induced subgraph of a $\overline{P_5}$-free graph. If any such induced subgraph already has the polynomial restricted-set outcome we are done; otherwise every large induced subgraph satisfies the hypothesis of the published complete-or-anticomplete blockade theorem, which then supplies the required polynomially large restricted set. Complement invariance transfers the result from $\overline{P_5}$ to $P_5$.

items.title: The five-vertex path and its complement have the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Read the previous theorem as the polynomial Rödl property of the singleton family $\{P_5\}$, and apply the published single-graph equivalence to get the Erdős–Hajnal property for $P_5$. The published complement-invariance proposition then gives the same property for $\overline{P_5}$.

title: Iterative Sparsification and the Five-Vertex Path — Examples

items.title: Two large anticonnected components give a complete two-blockade
items.strategy: Take a graph whose complement has two connected components of comparable size. Those two vertex sets are anticonnected in the original graph and complete to one another, so they realize the complete-blockade lemma directly.

items.title: A sparse $P_5$-free graph with an anticomplete two-blockade
items.strategy: Use the disjoint union of two short paths. The graph is $P_5$-free, sparse, and its two components themselves form an anticomplete blockade of length two.

items.title: An upside-down comb with anticonnected blocks creates a co-$P_5$
items.strategy: Take the five vertices named in the proof of the pure-blockade contraction lemma: the root, one tooth, one mixed vertex from another block, and two adjacent witnesses inside the first block. Their adjacencies are exactly those of $\overline{P_5}$.

items.title: A layout with a single wrong decided pair
items.strategy: Take two blocks meant to be anticomplete in the pattern graph, but place exactly one cross-edge between chosen vertices of the two blocks. That cross-edge is the unique wrong decided pair, making the bookkeeping in the layout argument concrete.
